titleEn: Two Days of Vomiting - Dehydration, Antiemetics and a Fluid Bolus

patient.name: Helen Marsh
patient.affectEn: Weak, pale and sweaty, semi-reclined on the sofa under a blanket with a plastic basin in her lap; retching at intervals; dizzy and miserable; does not try to get up.
patient.speechEn: Weak, short sentences ("I'm so dizzy... I can't stop being sick."); cooperative and answers only what she is asked; her daughter helps with the history and confirms her weight.

scene.settingEn: Ground-floor townhouse in Chilliwack at 0840 hrs. The daughter leads you to the living room: a warm room, no hazards, and the ambulance can park at the door. One patient: a 71-year-old woman semi-reclined on the sofa under a blanket, a plastic basin in her lap and vomit-stained towels on the floor. Chilliwack General Hospital is 11 minutes away.
hazardsEn: vomit and stool exposure - gloves and eye protection

bystanders.knowsEn: She called 911 and met you at the door. Her mother has vomited about 12 times in the last 24 hours (watery, never any blood) and has had about 6 loose watery stools since yesterday, with no blood and nothing black. She has kept no fluid down since last night and nearly fainted this morning on the way to the bathroom, with no head strike. Her mother's grandson had a stomach bug last week. Her mother weighs about 62 kg. She will collect her mother's medications (ramipril, hydrochlorothiazide, metformin) if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline, ondansetron, dimenhydrinate, methoxyflurane

dispatchEn: 0840 hrs. Code 3 to a ground-floor townhouse in Chilliwack. 71-year-old female with vomiting and diarrhea for two days, now too dizzy to stand. Her daughter called. Chilliwack General Hospital is 11 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch update en route: the daughter says her mother has not kept any fluid down since last night and nearly fainted on the way to the bathroom this morning.
arrivalEn: The patient's daughter meets you at the door of a ground-floor townhouse and leads you to the living room. The room is warm, there are no hazards, and the ambulance can park at the door. One patient.
firstLookEn: A woman semi-reclined on the sofa under a blanket, pale and sweaty, a plastic basin in her lap and vomit-stained towels on the floor. She is awake, looks weak and is retching into the basin.

primary.locEn: Alert (AVPU), GCS 15. Awake and speaking in short sentences: "I'm so dizzy... I can't stop being sick."
primary.airwayEn: Patent; she is speaking and retching into the basin. The vomit is watery yellow-green with no blood or coffee-ground material.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, shallow and regular, clear air entry on both sides, no accessory muscle use.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 118, weak and regular. Capillary refill is delayed at 4 seconds. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Modified rapid body survey for a medical patient: abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness around the umbilicus, no guarding or rigidity, not distended, no pulsatile mass. No signs of bleeding, no rash, no leg swelling. Skin cool, pale and clammy, with dry mucous membranes and poor turgor (skin is given automatically during the RBS).
primary.skinEn: cool, pale and clammy, with dry mucous membranes and poor turgor

history.ccEn: I can't stop being sick, and I'm so dizzy.

opqrst.oEn: It started two days ago. I've been sick about twelve times in the last day, and now it's only watery stuff, never any blood.
opqrst.pEn: It's worse whenever I try to drink anything. It eases off for a little while after I'm sick.
opqrst.rEn: Around my belly button. It doesn't go anywhere else.
opqrst.sEn: About a four out of ten.
opqrst.tEn: It started two days ago and it hasn't let up. The cramps come in waves.

history.painScoreEn: About a four out of ten.

sample.sEn: I can't stop being sick and I'm so dizzy. I'm dizzy when I stand and I nearly fainted this morning on the way to the bathroom - I didn't hit my head. I've been sick about twelve times in the last day, only watery stuff and never blood. I've had about six loose watery stools since yesterday, no blood and nothing black. I've only passed a small amount of dark urine since yesterday. I feel hot and cold but nobody has taken my temperature, and I have no chest pain.
sample.aEn: Penicillin - I get a rash. I've had Gravol before and had no reaction to it. No other allergies.
sample.mEn: Ramipril 5 milligrams once a day, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 milligrams once a day, and metformin 500 milligrams twice a day. I haven't kept any of them down since yesterday morning - I vomited them up. No blood thinners.
sample.pEn: High blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. No heart failure, no kidney or liver disease, no ulcers, no glaucoma, no asthma or COPD. No problem with my heart rhythm, nobody in my family has long QT, and I don't have phenylketonuria.
sample.lEn: I had a few sips of water at six this morning and vomited them within minutes. The last solid food was toast yesterday morning.
sample.eEn: My grandson had a stomach bug last week. Nothing else - I haven't hurt myself, and I didn't hit my head when I nearly fainted.

fe.generalEn: I've been tired and weak for two days, and I've felt hot and cold.
fe.cnsEn: I'm dizzy when I stand up. No headache and I'm not confused.
fe.respiratoryEn: No cough and no shortness of breath.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart races when I sit up. No chest pain and no swollen ankles.
fe.giGuEn: Crampy pain around the middle of my belly and I feel sick to my stomach. About twelve vomits and six watery stools. Only small amounts of dark urine. No blood in the vomit or the stool.
fe.integumentaryEn: My skin feels dry. No rash.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: I've had cramps in my calves. No joint pain.
fe.endocrineEn: Type 2 diabetes. I'm very thirsty, and I haven't checked my sugar at home for two days.
fe.eentEn: My mouth is dry and my lips are cracked. No change in my vision and no ear pain.

findings.headNeckEn: Dry mucous membranes and tongue, sunken eyes, neck veins flat, trachea midline, no neck stiffness.
findings.chestLungsEn: Clear, with equal air entry at all 6 sites.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft, with mild diffuse tenderness around the umbilicus. No guarding or rebound, not distended, active bowel sounds, no pulsatile mass.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Pedal pulses weak but present, feet cool, no swelling, calves soft and non-tender, movement and sensation intact.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Radial pulses weak, skin tents slowly on the forearm, movement and sensation intact.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, baseline before any fluid or antiemetic; BP is taken supine - she is not sat or stood for an orthostatic check

resp.character: regular, clear air entry on both sides, no accessory muscle use

vitalsSets.skin: cool, pale, clammy, dry mucous membranes, poor turgor, capillary refill 4 seconds
vitalsSets.spo2: 95% on room air, 98% on 15 L NRB

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: about 6 minutes after set 1, en route, with NO fluid running (EMR path, or a PCP who has not started the bolus): stays near baseline
about 6 minutes after set 1, en route, with the first 500 mL of the bolus running (roughly 250 mL in; ondansetron onset is 15-30 minutes, so the nausea is unchanged): improving but not corrected

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: She retches and vomits a small amount of watery fluid into the basin.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan oxygen, suction, a basin, blankets and (PCP) the IV and fluid set-up; anticipate dehydration or shock in an older patient
triggers: bringing oxygen suction and a basin
bring the suction and a basin
I'll set up for an IV and fluids

expected.actionEn: Recognize from dispatch that near-fainting after two days of vomiting may be an unstable hypovolemia call, not 'just the flu'
triggers: near fainting means she may be unstable
this is more than a stomach bug

expected.actionEn: Anticipate vomit and stool exposure: gloves and eye protection ready
Verbalize hazards (none), environment, nature of illness (vomiting and diarrhea, possible infectious gastroenteritis), number of patients (1)
triggers: nature of illness is vomiting and diarrhea
ambulance can park at the door

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection (vomit splash risk)
triggers: putting on gloves and eye protection

expected.actionEn: First look: pale, sweaty, weak, semi-reclined with a basin and soiled towels - looks dehydrated and unwell
Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert, GCS 15 - and state that any drift toward drowsiness would be a worsening sign
triggers: do you know where you are
drowsiness would be a worsening sign

expected.actionEn: Verbalize c-spine not indicated (medical, no trauma)
Assess airway; she is retching, so keep suction and the basin within reach and check the vomit for blood
triggers: she's talking so the airway is clear

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing - rate, depth, air entry both sides, accessory muscle use; no respiratory distress
Assess circulation - weak rapid radial pulse (118) and delayed capillary refill (4 seconds) mean poor perfusion; no external bleeding
Perform a modified rapid body survey with a gentle abdominal exam - look for a pulsatile mass, guarding, bleeding and other causes of shock
triggers: look for other causes of shock
check for bleeding and a pulsatile mass

expected.actionEn: Note skin: cool, pale, clammy, dry mucous membranes, poor turgor
High-flow oxygen 15 L by non-rebreather - high flow is required in shock - and keep SpO2 at or above 94%
Position supine to support blood pressure and keep her warm, with suction and the basin at hand and a plan to turn her onto her side if she vomits
triggers: supine to support her blood pressure

expected.actionEn: Categorize as RTC and name the criterion: cool, pale, clammy skin secondary to suspected shock (p.7), not 'just the flu'
triggers: cool pale clammy skin means unstable

expected.actionEn: Packaged supine, warm and ready to load within 15 minutes, with the secondary survey done en route
triggers: do the secondary survey in the ambulance

expected.actionEn: Delegate: the partner brings the stretcher, the daughter collects the medications; the patient is moved on the stretcher and never walked
triggers: get the stretcher to the sofa
ask her daughter to collect her medications
daughter, can you get her pills
we'll move her on the stretcher

expected.actionEn: Establish chief complaint: two days of vomiting with dizziness and weakness
HxC/C with OPQRST and quantify the fluid loss: about 12 vomits in 24 hours, about 6 watery stools, scant dark urine, no intake, near-fainting, sick contact, no blood in vomit or stool
triggers: how many times have you vomited

expected.actionEn: Pain scale: crampy periumbilical pain 4/10
PMHx, asking the pertinent negatives for the drugs she may need: hypertension and diabetes; no heart rhythm problem or family long QT, no glaucoma, no asthma/COPD, no ulcer or liver disease
triggers: any history of ulcers or liver disease

expected.actionEn: Medications: ramipril, hydrochlorothiazide, metformin, none kept down since yesterday morning, no blood thinners
triggers: what do you take for your blood pressure

expected.actionEn: Allergies: penicillin (rash); no prior reaction to dimenhydrinate (Gravol)
LOI: sips of water at 0600 and vomited; no solid food since yesterday morning
triggers: anything to eat or drink today

expected.actionEn: Ask her weight (about 62 kg) from the daughter - needed for the 20 mL/kg bolus and any weight-based antiemetic dose (PCP)
GCS with components (15: E4 V5 M6)
BP by auscultation, supine - recognize a systolic under 90 as the Hypovolemia protocol criterion and do not stand her for orthostatics
Pulse rate/strength/rhythm - rapid and weak
Respirations rate/depth/character
Skin hands-on: temperature, colour, moisture, turgor, mucous membranes, capillary refill
Pupils
SpO2 with calibration, noting the reading before and after oxygen
BGL - indicated: older diabetic on metformin who has barely eaten for two days
Temperature - indicated: gastroenteritis with possible infection
FE - General health
FE - CNS
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (vomits, stools, urine output, any blood)
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine (diabetes pertinent)
FE - EENT
Head/neck exam: mucous membranes, eyes, neck veins, trachea
Chest exam with 6-site auscultation, recorded as the baseline before fluid
triggers: baseline lung sounds before the fluid

expected.actionEn: Abdomen exam: tenderness, guarding, distension, pulsatile mass
Back exam
Lower extremities: pulses, temperature, swelling, calves, CSM
Upper extremities: radial pulses, skin turgor, CSM, and choose the IV site

Start the Hypovolemia protocol only with the indications confirmed and baseline vitals complete: fluid loss (about 12 vomits, 6 watery stools, no intake), systolic 86 (under 90) and other signs of shock (cool clammy skin, pulse 118, capillary refill 4 seconds)
triggers: systolic under 90 with signs of shock

expected.actionEn: Airway management for a vomiting patient: suction and basin within reach, supine for blood pressure but ready to turn her onto her side, suction any vomit at once
triggers: turn her on her side if she vomits
roll her to the side if she vomits

expected.actionEn: Rule out each analgesic aloud and withhold them all (at PCP level including methoxyflurane, which is limited to hemodynamically stable patients): Entonox (shock caution, causes nausea and vomiting), acetaminophen (hypovolemia caution, vomiting is a listed overdose symptom so the cause must be clear, no tablet will stay down), ibuprofen (cannot keep an oral tablet down); document the reasons
triggers: no Entonox because of the shock
no methoxyflurane because she is hypotensive

expected.actionEn: Nothing by mouth; say that the IV, the fluid bolus and the antiemetic are PCP additions and that at EMR level the care is oxygen, position, warmth and rapid transport
triggers: IV and fluids are PCP level
the PCP will start the IV
EMR care is oxygen position warmth and transport

expected.actionEn: PCP: IV with aseptic technique, then the NS bolus calculated from the weight - 62 kg x 20 mL/kg = 1,240 mL, never above 2 L - given in 500 mL steps

PCP: give the antiemetic en route only after ruling out its contraindications aloud - ondansetron 4 mg PO (allergy, congenital long QT in her and her family, phenylketonuria) or dimenhydrinate 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg (hypersensitivity; elderly and hypertension cautions)
triggers: any long QT in the family

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs (including breath sounds), the IV site and the bolus after every move and after each 500 mL
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes; interpret the trend out loud as improving but not yet corrected
Reassess after every 500 mL against the systolic target of 90 and complete the 20 mL/kg (1,240 mL) in 500 mL steps - not an open-ended or fixed volume
Manage the vomit that happens during the set: suction and turn her onto her side, then resume the vitals
Reassess the pain (4/10) and the nausea, and document that Entonox and oral analgesics stay withheld and why
En-route notification for a critical patient: age, shock from fluid loss, blood pressure, treatment started
Complete hand-off with weight, fluid loss, vitals trend, fluid volume and time, antiemetic and time, and the analgesics withheld with reasons
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes with drug and fluid times and the reasons Entonox and oral analgesics were withheld

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate stands her up, sits her up for an orthostatic blood pressure check, lets her walk, or walks her to the stretcher or ambulance (any self-exertion). Sitting her up for a moment so she can vomit is NOT this event.
candidate positions her supine / lays her flat to support her blood pressure (also report the patient-position item)

candidate leaves her semi-reclined or sitting up for the whole call, or sits her up for transport, and never positions her supine although she is hypotensive. Turning her briefly onto her side to vomit is NOT this event.

candidate gives her anything by mouth - water, an oral rehydration drink, food or a tablet - other than the ondansetron 4 mg PO a PCP may give (also report the drug event for any medication). Saying nothing by mouth is NOT this event.
an EMR candidate actually starts an IV or runs IV fluid (also report the drug event). Saying the IV and fluid are PCP skills is NOT this event.

candidate delays loading or transport on scene to start an IV, run fluid, give an antiemetic or finish the full head-to-toe, instead of loading first and treating en route (unstable patients are treated en route). The primary survey and baseline vital signs are NOT this event.

candidate chooses a nasal cannula or a low-flow mask for her, or says she needs no oxygen because the SpO2 reads 95%, although she is in shock and high flow by non-rebreather is required. Putting her on the non-rebreather is NOT this event.

candidate actually administers oral glucose, glucagon or D10W (also report the drug event) although her BGL is 5.2 mmol/L. Asking whether glucose is indicated, or saying it is withheld, is NOT this event.

candidate asks about, or states that they have ruled out, ondansetron's contraindications: congenital long QT or other heart rhythm problems in her or her family, phenylketonuria, or an ondansetron allergy

candidate asks about, or states that they have ruled out, dimenhydrinate's contraindication or cautions: hypersensitivity or allergy (including an earlier reaction to Gravol), glaucoma, prostate or urinary obstruction
PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL, or onto the next 500 mL, without reassessing her (BP / vitals / breath sounds / ABCs) in between
PCP orders or runs a bolus that is not 20 mL/kg of her weight - for example a fixed 1 L or 2 L, a wide-open run with no calculation, or a total above the 2 L maximum. Her 62 kg gives 1,240 mL.

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this call: shock is a listed caution, and nausea and vomiting are listed adverse effects in a patient who is already vomiting
500-1,000 mg PO - WITHHELD in this call: hypovolemia is a listed caution, vomiting is a listed symptom of overdose so the cause must be clear, and she cannot keep a tablet down
300-400 mg PO - WITHHELD in this call: an oral tablet cannot be retained while she vomits every few minutes
3 mL self-administered via inhaler - WITHHELD in this call: limited to conscious, hemodynamically stable patients, cardiac instability is a listed caution and she is hypotensive
PCP: after vascular access en route, bolus 20 mL/kg IV to a maximum of 2 L, in 500 mL steps, reassessing after each and aiming for a systolic of 90; her 62 kg gives 1,240 mL
PCP: 4 mg PO (adult) for nausea and vomiting once the IV is running and its contraindications are ruled out: allergy, congenital long QT in her and her family, phenylketonuria; onset 15-30 minutes
PCP: 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg (50 mg here), IV diluted with NS over about 2 minutes or IM undiluted; contraindication hypersensitivity; cautions elderly and hypertension
PCP: NOT indicated in this call - her shock is from fluid loss, not blood loss
15 g PO - NOT indicated: her BGL is 5.2 mmol/L and she is vomiting
NOT indicated: her BGL is 5.2 mmol/L
PCP: NOT indicated: her BGL is 5.2 mmol/L

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR gives high-flow oxygen (required in shock), supine positioning with suction and a basin ready, warmth, nothing by mouth, a full baseline set including BGL and temperature, a clear RTC decision with the criterion named, and rapid transport. EMR does NOT start an IV, give a fluid bolus, or give ondansetron or dimenhydrinate - those are PCP additions - so without fluid set 2 stays near baseline (BP 88/54, pulse 116, respirations 24). Entonox and all oral analgesics are withheld at both levels, with the reasons said aloud. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds, en route, vascular access with aseptic technique, a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus (62 kg = 1,240 mL, maximum 2 L, reassess after every 500 mL, target systolic 90), an antiemetic once its contraindications are ruled out (ondansetron 4 mg PO, or dimenhydrinate 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg) and the 9-system Functional Enquiry. TXA is not indicated: this is fluid loss, not blood loss. Textbook practice - not a BC rubric item: ibuprofen is also unwise here because dehydration with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic stresses the kidneys, and an ODT tablet dissolves on the tongue, which is why an oral antiemetic is still reasonable in a patient who is vomiting.

sourcePages: Scenario md-11 (data/practical/scenarios-2.json): dispatch, scene, primary (alert, shock from fluid loss, soft tender abdomen), transport (RTC), history (patient and daughter), vitals sets 1-2 (set 2 EMR path without fluid; improving path with the bolus running), FE, exam, interventions (analgesia trap, PCP bolus and antiemetic), ongoing (vomit during the set), handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (cool pale clammy skin secondary to suspected shock); p.11 primary-survey interventions (airway maintenance and suctioning, oxygen for evidence of shock); p.13 AVPU; p.38 IV Procedures (aseptic technique, replace fluids due to hypovolemia); p.48 Nausea - Vomiting (position of comfort consistent with protecting the airway; PCP dimenhydrinate or ondansetron, fluid bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 litres reassessing every 500 mL, target systolic 90; unstable patients treated en route; suction ready); p.50 Oxygen Administration (shock requires high-flow oxygen); p.54 Hypovolemia (indications: hypovolemia, systolic under 90, other signs of shock; supine, warm, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above; PCP vascular access en route, fluid bolus; TXA only for blood loss); p.58-59 Acetaminophen (do not give if overdose suspected - nausea, vomiting; caution hypovolemia); p.63 Dimenhydrinate (1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg; hypersensitivity; cautions elderly, hypertension); p.65 Entonox (cautions shock; adverse effects nausea and vomiting); p.68 Ibuprofen; p.71 Methoxyflurane (conscious, hemodynamically stable patients; cautions cardiac instability); p.75 Ondansetron (4 mg PO; contraindications allergy, congenital long QT, PKU). Grading criteria p.19 (packaging goal times), p.35 (vitals intervals).
